lead.headline: Three Leaders, One Room in Shenzhen, and No Seat for Europe
lead.deck: Trump says he will raise Ukraine with Xi and Putin. Kyiv warns against a new Yalta, and the EU says a ceasefire must come first.
body: On Thursday, in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, the leaders of the United States, China and Russia are due to meet together for the first time ever. Their subject is nuclear stockpiles: the last nuclear arms treaty between the US and Russia expired in February 2026. A White House official said no disarmament deal is expected; the meeting is a starting point. China, which calls the meeting “ground-breaking,” has long insisted that the US and Russia cut their own large arsenals first. No European government will be in the room.

Ukraine may come up anyway. US officials had said Donald Trump would avoid the war, but Trump says he will raise it with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, along with the war in Iran. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned against a repeat of the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the US, Britain and the Soviet Union divided Germany into occupation zones. The Kremlin replies that any Shenzhen agreements cannot be enforced on others.

Europe is preparing its own voice. After a meeting in Dublin, leaders agreed that the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, with European Council and NATO officials, will speak for Europe in future peace talks. The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, has set out its condition: “A ceasefire must come first.”

lead.why: Ukraine’s future decides how safe the rest of Europe feels. When the biggest nuclear powers talk without Europe, its governments have to be heard in other ways: by choosing who speaks for them, and by setting conditions of their own.

world.headline: A Router Swap in Arkansas Grounded Every Departure in the US
world.deck: Flights are close to normal again, and Washington is arguing over who pays to replace an ageing network.
body: Friday 13 November showed how much air travel depends on a network most passengers never see. At 3:36 p.m. Eastern Time, America’s Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted departures across the country, ordering a nationwide ground stop after its communications network became unstable. Roughly 3,500 aircraft were already airborne; every one of them came down safely. The FAA’s chief, Bryan Bedford, said the stop was ordered “out of an abundance of caution.”

Officials said there was no sign of a cyberattack. Instead, the trouble began with an upgrade. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a worker for L3Harris, the defence firm that owns and operates the network tying US air traffic control together, was swapping old copper wire for fiber and replacing a router at a remote site: a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. Once switched on, the new router bombarded its neighbours with about 1,000 log-on attempts every four to five seconds, and the system overloaded, disrupting communications at 17 of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers. A similar upgrade at a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, weeks earlier had added to the strain.

Departures resumed at about 8:20 p.m., after more than four hours. The last nationwide stop came in January 2023, when an FAA computer system failed, and the one before that after the 11 September 2001 attacks. The flight-tracking service FlightAware counted about 9,159 cancellations on Friday alone. By Monday most major airlines were running normally or close to it.

The argument that follows is about money. Duffy called the $12.5 billion down payment for modernising the system not enough, and the administration now wants $30 billion. Two members of Congress, Rick Larsen and Andre Carson, countered that only $1 billion of the $12.5 billion has been used. Bedford says about 70% of the network has already moved from copper to fiber.

uk.headline: Burnham Readies a Brexit Verdict Before Facing EU Leaders
uk.deck: Four days before his first UK-EU summit, the Prime Minister was due to argue Britain has “lost more than we have gained”.
body: In 2016, 52% of British voters chose to leave the EU. On Monday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was due to tell the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in the City of London that the move has not paid off: “We have lost more than we have gained.” His complaint is that a “needlessly hard” exit raised barriers for firms that sell to EU countries.

The real test comes on Friday 20 November in Brussels, at Burnham’s first formal summit with EU leaders. There he is expected to sign agreements covering food, energy and a youth scheme under which young Britons could study and work in EU countries, and young Europeans in Britain. He puts the gain for the British economy at about $22.5 billion, roughly 0.4% of GDP.

Brussels has demands of its own. The EU dislikes Britain’s call for a yearly limit on the youth scheme, and wants its students at British universities charged the lower “home” fees. At home, the Conservatives say Labour is “dragging us into the European Union via the back door,” leaving Britain to follow EU rules it cannot shape.

europe.headline: EU Hits Nearly 50 Russian Banks and Sends Kyiv Its Biggest Payment Yet
europe.deck: “We have leverage,” says Kaja Kallas, as the EU uses money to earn a say in how the war ends.
body: Sanctions let a government punish people and companies without fighting: their assets in the EU are frozen, and EU businesses may not give them money. On Monday, EU foreign ministers in Brussels added 113 names to their sanctions on Russia, including nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, to cut off “the financial channels” that fund the war.

Money flowed the other way too. Ministers approved nearly 8 billion euros for Ukraine, the largest single payment so far from the Ukraine Facility, a fund offering more than 50 billion euros through 2027. About 5 billion euros of it comes from the Ukraine Support Loan, and Kyiv completed more than 20 reform steps to unlock it. Once it arrives, payments since mid-2024 will pass 40 billion euros.

The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, who chaired the meeting, said Russia’s demands are “a clear pretext for keeping the war going.” Europe’s tools, she said, are “our sanctions” and “frozen assets.”

sports.body: England beat world champions Spain 3-2 in Madrid in the Nations League on Sunday, ending a 43-match unbeaten run. lead.headline: Three Big Leaders Meet, Without Europe
body: The leaders of the United States, China and Russia are due to meet on Thursday. It will be the first time ever. They meet in Shenzhen, a city in southern China. They will talk about nuclear weapons.

President Trump says he will also talk about the war in Ukraine. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, is worried. He has warned against a repeat of Yalta in 1945, when big powers divided up Germany.
No European country will be at the meeting. Europe has picked five countries to speak for it in future peace talks. The EU says a ceasefire, which means a stop to the fighting, must come first.

world.headline: A Broken Router Stopped US Flights
body: On 13 November, no planes could take off anywhere in the United States. About 3,500 planes were already flying. They all landed safely.
A worker was replacing a router, a machine that passes messages between computers. The new router sent out far too many messages. The network that air traffic control uses got overloaded.
Planes could fly again after more than four hours. By Monday most airlines were back to normal. The government now says it needs more money to replace old equipment.

uk.headline: Britain’s Leader Says Brexit Has Not Worked
body: In 2016, 52% of voters chose to leave the European Union. This is called Brexit.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham was due to give a speech on Monday. He planned to say Britain has lost more than it gained by leaving.

On Friday he goes to Brussels. He is expected to sign deals on food and energy. Another deal would let young people study and work in each other’s countries. Some details are still being argued about. The Conservatives say Labour is taking Britain back towards the EU.

europe.headline: The EU Punishes Russian Banks and Helps Ukraine
body: Sanctions are punishments that do not use weapons. The money of people on the list is frozen in the EU.
On Monday the EU added 113 names to its list against Russia. Nearly 50 are banks and money companies. The EU wants to cut off the money that pays for Russia’s war.
The EU also approved nearly 8 billion euros for Ukraine. It is the biggest single payment from this fund. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, says sanctions give Europe power in the war.
